claim: In mammals, mothers are essential for the early development of their infants since they provide postnatal care.
source: In mammals, mothers are essential for the early development of their infants since they provide postnatal care (Maestripieri and Mateo, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Maestripieri and Mateo, 2009.

claim: Maternal loss in mammals reduces growth.
source: Maternal loss in mammals reduces growth (Samuni et al., 2020), survival (Watts et al., 2009; Andres et al., 2013; Tung et al., 2016; Stanton et al., 2020), and long-term reproductive success (Andres et al., 2013; Strauss et al., 2020; Crockford et al., 2020; Zipple et al., 2021, reviewed in Clutton-Brock, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Samuni et al., 2020.

claim: Maternal loss in mammals reduces survival.
source: Maternal loss in mammals reduces growth (Samuni et al., 2020), survival (Watts et al., 2009; Andres et al., 2013; Tung et al., 2016; Stanton et al., 2020), and long-term reproductive success (Andres et al., 2013; Strauss et al., 2020; Crockford et al., 2020; Zipple et al., 2021, reviewed in Clutton-Brock, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Watts et al., 2009; Andres et al., 2013; Tung et al., 2016; Stanton et al., 2020.

claim: Maternal loss in mammals reduces long-term reproductive success.
source: Maternal loss in mammals reduces growth (Samuni et al., 2020), survival (Watts et al., 2009; Andres et al., 2013; Tung et al., 2016; Stanton et al., 2020), and long-term reproductive success (Andres et al., 2013; Strauss et al., 2020; Crockford et al., 2020; Zipple et al., 2021, reviewed in Clutton-Brock, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Andres et al., 2013; Strauss et al., 2020; Crockford et al., 2020; Zipple et al., 2021, reviewed in Clutton-Brock, 2016.

claim: The biological embedding model (BEM) posits that adversity experienced early in life, including exposure to severe stressors, can have deleterious consequences on an individual's physiology and health across their lifespan.
source: The biological embedding model (BEM; Power and Hertzman, 1997; Miller et al., 2011; Berens et al., 2017) posits that adversity experienced early in life, including exposure to severe stressors, can have deleterious consequences on an individual's physiology and health across their lifespan.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Power and Hertzman, 1997; Miller et al., 2011; Berens et al., 2017.

claim: Early-life adversity impacts several interconnected physiological pathways among which the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis plays a central role.
source: Early-life adversity impacts several interconnected physiological pathways (reviewed in Berens et al., 2017) among which the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis plays a central role (Miller et al., 2009; Miller et al., 2011; Taylor et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Berens et al., 2017; Miller et al., 2009; Miller et al., 2011; Taylor et al., 2011.

claim: The HPA axis is activated in response to internal physiological challenges and external stressors through a chain of reactions, known as the 'stress response' or 'reactive homeostasis', which also results in the release of glucocorticoids.
source: The HPA axis is activated in response to internal physiological challenges and external stressors through a chain of reactions, known as the 'stress response' or 'reactive homeostasis' (Romero et al., 2009), which also results in the release of glucocorticoids (Sapolsky, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Romero et al., 2009 and Sapolsky, 2002.

claim: The stress response is adaptive: it stimulates the release of energy out of storage in the form of glucose, and it increases cardiovascular circulation and respiratory rate, allowing organisms to respond to acute stressors such as predators.
source: Overall, this response is adaptive (Charmandari et al., 2005): it stimulates the release of energy out of storage in the form of glucose, and it increases cardiovascular circulation and respiratory rate, allowing organisms to respond to acute stressors such as predators (Sapolsky, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Charmandari et al., 2005 and Sapolsky, 2002.

claim: Exposure to harsh social conditions during childhood, such as those that can result from maternal loss, may lead to repeated and prolonged activation of the HPA axis early in life.
source: Exposure to harsh social conditions during childhood, such as those that can result from maternal loss, may lead to repeated and prolonged activation of the HPA axis early in life.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the context of the BEM framework.

claim: Repeated and prolonged activation of the HPA axis early in life may result in long-term HPA axis dysfunction (i.e., either hypo- or hyper-responsiveness to stressor).
source: These activations provide an adaptive physiological response by mobilizing energy that helps children to cope with the immediate socioecological challenges but may result in long-term HPA axis dysfunction (i.e., either hypo- or hyper-responsiveness to stressor; Miller et al., 2011; Ehrlich et al., 2016; Berens et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Miller et al., 2011; Ehrlich et al., 2016; Berens et al., 2017.

claim: The HPA axis is considered to be at the core of the link between early-life adversity and fitness since repeated activation of the HPA axis over prolonged periods (chronic stress) and/or HPA axis malfunctioning can have detrimental effects on individual overall health.
source: The HPA axis is considered to be at the core of the link between early-life adversity and fitness since repeated activation of the HPA axis over prolonged periods (chronic stress) and/or HPA axis malfunctioning can have detrimental effects on individual overall health (Sapolsky, 2002; Slavich and Cole, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sapolsky, 2002; Slavich and Cole, 2013.

claim: Over- and/or prolonged activation of the HPA axis is known to suppress the immune system.
source: For instance, over- and/or prolonged activation of the HPA axis is known to suppress the immune system (Grossman, 1985; Setchell et al., 2010; Slavich and Cole, 2013) and reduce survival (Campos et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Grossman, 1985; Setchell et al., 2010; Slavich and Cole, 2013.

claim: Over- and/or prolonged activation of the HPA axis is known to reduce survival.
source: For instance, over- and/or prolonged activation of the HPA axis is known to suppress the immune system (Grossman, 1985; Setchell et al., 2010; Slavich and Cole, 2013) and reduce survival (Campos et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Campos et al., 2021.

claim: The HPA axis mediates some of the observed negative effects of early-life adversity on the immune response, such as elevated levels of inflammatory markers in the blood.
source: The HPA axis also mediates some of the observed negative effects of early-life adversity on the immune response, such as elevated levels of inflammatory markers in the blood (Danese et al., 2011; Ehrlich et al., 2016; Rasmussen et al., 2019, reviewed in Berens et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Danese et al., 2011; Ehrlich et al., 2016; Rasmussen et al., 2019, reviewed in Berens et al., 2017.

claim: The adaptive calibration model (ACM) proposes that intra- and interindividual changes in stress responsivity are mainly always adaptive, allowing individuals to adjust their physiology during development to respond to changes in the social and ecological environment.
source: An alternative framework, the adaptive calibration model (ACM), proposes that intra- and interindividual changes in stress responsivity are mainly always adaptive, allowing individuals to adjust their physiology during development to respond to changes in the social and ecological environment (Del Giudice et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Del Giudice et al., 2011.

claim: According to the ACM, modification of the HPA axis activity in response to maternal loss should be sensitive to the phase of development at which maternal loss occurred, especially in long-lived species with an extended immature period.
source: According to the ACM, modification of the HPA axis activity in response to maternal loss should be sensitive to the phase of development at which maternal loss occurred, especially in long-lived species with an extended immature period.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the ACM framework described in the manuscript.

claim: In humans, maternal loss leads to short- and long-term alterations of the HPA axis functioning.
source: In humans, maternal loss leads to short- and long-term alterations of the HPA axis functioning (Heim and Nemeroff, 2001; Sánchez et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Heim and Nemeroff, 2001; Sánchez et al., 2001.

claim: In humans, cortisol levels follow a diurnal pattern characterized by an early morning peak (awakening response) and a regular decline throughout the day.
source: In humans, cortisol levels follow a diurnal pattern characterized by an early morning peak (awakening response) and a regular decline throughout the day (Doman et al., 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Doman et al., 1986.

claim: Diurnal cortisol slopes, as well as the cortisol-awakening response specifically, serve as health markers.
source: These diurnal cortisol slopes, as well as the cortisol-awakening response specifically, serve as health markers.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Deviations from stereotypical patterns of high morning and low evening cortisol levels (i.e., flatter diurnal slopes) are typically interpreted as indications of pathology and HPA axis dysregulation and/or a marker of chronic stress in human clinical studies.
source: Deviations from stereotypical patterns of high morning and low evening cortisol levels (i.e., flatter diurnal slopes) are typically interpreted as indications of pathology and HPA axis dysregulation and/or a marker of chronic stress in human clinical studies (Pruessner et al., 1999; Sánchez et al., 2001; Clow et al., 2004; Kudielka et al., 2006; Miller et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pruessner et al., 1999; Sánchez et al., 2001; Clow et al., 2004; Kudielka et al., 2006; Miller et al., 2007.

claim: Flattening of diurnal cortisol slopes reflects a compression in the dynamic range of the HPA axis functioning that is indicative of a reduced ability to respond appropriately to stressors and to downregulate hormonal stress levels.
source: Flattening of diurnal cortisol slopes reflects a compression in the dynamic range of the HPA axis functioning (Karlamangla et al., 2019) that is indicative of a reduced ability to respond appropriately to stressors and to downregulate hormonal stress levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Karlamangla et al., 2019 and inference about the implications.

claim: Flatter diurnal cortisol slopes are associated with reduced survival in humans.
source: Flatter diurnal cortisol slopes are even associated with direct fitness costs in humans such as reduced survival (Sephton et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sephton et al., 2000.

claim: In humans, orphaned children typically exhibit lower cortisol-awakening responses or higher evening cortisol levels than mother-reared children, leading to overall flatter diurnal cortisol slopes.
source: In humans, orphaned children typically exhibit lower cortisol-awakening responses (Carlson and Earls, 1997) or higher evening cortisol levels (Gunnar et al., 2001) than mother-reared children, leading to overall flatter diurnal cortisol slopes (Carlson and Earls, 1997; Tarullo and Gunnar, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Carlson and Earls, 1997; Gunnar et al., 2001; Tarullo and Gunnar, 2006.

claim: Flatter diurnal slopes and/or lower morning cortisol levels are observed in children experiencing other forms of early-life adversity, such as maltreatment by parents, parental divorce, or placement in foster families.
source: Flatter diurnal slopes and/or lower morning cortisol levels are also observed in children experiencing other forms of early-life adversity, such as maltreatment by parents, parental divorce, or placement in foster families (Kaufman, 1991; Hart et al., 1996; Meinlschmidt and Heim, 2005; Dozier et al., 2006; Bernard et al., 2015; McLachlan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kaufman, 1991; Hart et al., 1996; Meinlschmidt and Heim, 2005; Dozier et al., 2006; Bernard et al., 2015; McLachlan et al., 2016.

claim: Maternal loss can be associated with generally higher cortisol levels throughout the day.
source: Beyond diurnal cortisol patterns, maternal loss can also be associated with generally higher cortisol levels throughout the day (Gunnar et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gunnar et al., 2001.

claim: Several studies in humans document long-lasting effects of early-life adversity, including maternal loss, on children's HPA axis functioning.
source: In support of the BEM, several studies in humans document long-lasting effects of early-life adversity, including maternal loss, on children's HPA axis functioning.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the studies cited in the following sentences.

claim: Adults up to 64 years old who experienced mistreatment and/or the loss of one or both parents during childhood have, depending on the study, a lower or higher cortisol-awakening response.
source: Adults up to 64 years old who experienced mistreatment and/or the loss of one or both parents during childhood have, depending on the study, a lower (Meinlschmidt and Heim, 2005; Kawai et al., 2017) or higher cortisol-awakening response (Gonzalez et al., 2009; Butler et al., 2017), flatter diurnal cortisol slopes (Karlamangla et al., 2019), and generally higher cortisol levels throughout the day (Nicolson, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Meinlschmidt and Heim, 2005; Kawai et al., 2017; Gonzalez et al., 2009; Butler et al., 2017.

claim: Adults up to 64 years old who experienced mistreatment and/or the loss of one or both parents during childhood have flatter diurnal cortisol slopes.
source: Adults up to 64 years old who experienced mistreatment and/or the loss of one or both parents during childhood have, depending on the study, a lower (Meinlschmidt and Heim, 2005; Kawai et al., 2017) or higher cortisol-awakening response (Gonzalez et al., 2009; Butler et al., 2017), flatter diurnal cortisol slopes (Karlamangla et al., 2019), and generally higher cortisol levels throughout the day (Nicolson, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Karlamangla et al., 2019.

claim: Adults up to 64 years old who experienced mistreatment and/or the loss of one or both parents during childhood have generally higher cortisol levels throughout the day.
source: Adults up to 64 years old who experienced mistreatment and/or the loss of one or both parents during childhood have, depending on the study, a lower (Meinlschmidt and Heim, 2005; Kawai et al., 2017) or higher cortisol-awakening response (Gonzalez et al., 2009; Butler et al., 2017), flatter diurnal cortisol slopes (Karlamangla et al., 2019), and generally higher cortisol levels throughout the day (Nicolson, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nicolson, 2004.

claim: Human orphans adopted at an early age presented diurnal cortisol excretion profiles comparable to children raised by their biological parents.
source: In support of the ACM, human orphans adopted at an early age presented diurnal cortisol excretion profiles comparable to children raised by their biological parents (Gunnar et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gunnar et al., 2001.

claim: Orphans placed for extended periods in orphanages in which they were exposed to drastic food restriction and physical violence presented higher cortisol levels than mother-reared children, particularly in the evening.
source: In contrast, orphans placed for extended periods in orphanages in which they were exposed to drastic food restriction and physical violence presented higher cortisol levels than mother-reared children, particularly in the evening (Gunnar et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gunnar et al., 2001.

claim: Orphan bonobo immatures raised in sanctuaries by surrogate human mothers presented similar cortisol levels to mother-reared immatures.
source: Orphan bonobo immatures raised in sanctuaries by surrogate human mothers presented similar cortisol levels to mother-reared immatures (Wobber and Hare, 2011), whereas nursery-reared orphan macaques, without surrogate mothers, presented blunted morning cortisol levels (Thomas et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wobber and Hare, 2011.

claim: Nursery-reared orphan macaques, without surrogate mothers, presented blunted morning cortisol levels.
source: Orphan bonobo immatures raised in sanctuaries by surrogate human mothers presented similar cortisol levels to mother-reared immatures (Wobber and Hare, 2011), whereas nursery-reared orphan macaques, without surrogate mothers, presented blunted morning cortisol levels (Thomas et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Thomas et al., 1995.

claim: A study on wild female baboons showed that simultaneous exposure to several forms of early-life adversity, and some isolated forms of adversity such as drought and low maternal rank, leads to an overall elevation in glucocorticoid levels in adulthood.
source: A study on wild female baboons, using extensive long-term data, showed that simultaneous exposure to several forms of early-life adversity, and some isolated forms of adversity such as drought and low maternal rank, leads to an overall elevation in glucocorticoid levels in adulthood (Rosenbaum et al., 2020), offering support for the BEM.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rosenbaum et al., 2020.

claim: Maternal loss in isolation did not lead to long-term elevation of glucocorticoid levels in wild female baboons.
source: However, maternal loss in isolation did not lead to long-term elevation of glucocorticoid levels, suggesting that baboons may have buffering mechanisms to offset the effects of biological embedding for some forms of early-life adversity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study on baboons cited in the previous sentence (Rosenbaum et al., 2020).

claim: Baboons start reproducing 3–4 years after weaning.
source: Baboons start reproducing 3–4 years after weaning, whereas humans and great apes, including chimpanzees, share an extended juvenile phase between weaning and first reproduction (Wittig and Boesch, 2019a).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about baboon life history.

claim: Humans and great apes, including chimpanzees, share an extended juvenile phase between weaning and first reproduction.
source: Baboons start reproducing 3–4 years after weaning, whereas humans and great apes, including chimpanzees, share an extended juvenile phase between weaning and first reproduction (Wittig and Boesch, 2019a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wittig and Boesch, 2019a.

claim: Diurnal cortisol slopes are repeatable in adult chimpanzees (i.e., are consistent within a given individual over time).
source: In chimpanzees, these slopes are repeatable in adults (i.e., are consistent within a given individual over time, Sonnweber et al., 2018) but also show plasticity to physiological challenges such as disease outbreaks (Behringer et al., 2020) or aging (Emery Thompson et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sonnweber et al., 2018.

claim: Diurnal cortisol slopes in chimpanzees show plasticity to physiological challenges such as disease outbreaks.
source: In chimpanzees, these slopes are repeatable in adults (i.e., are consistent within a given individual over time, Sonnweber et al., 2018) but also show plasticity to physiological challenges such as disease outbreaks (Behringer et al., 2020) or aging (Emery Thompson et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Behringer et al., 2020.

claim: Diurnal cortisol slopes in chimpanzees show plasticity to aging.
source: In chimpanzees, these slopes are repeatable in adults (i.e., are consistent within a given individual over time, Sonnweber et al., 2018) but also show plasticity to physiological challenges such as disease outbreaks (Behringer et al., 2020) or aging (Emery Thompson et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Emery Thompson et al., 2020.

claim: Wild chimpanzees are known to provide social support to orphaned individuals, ranging from tolerance in feeding sites to full adoptions.
source: Wild chimpanzees are known to provide social support to orphaned individuals, ranging from tolerance in feeding sites to full adoptions (i.e., daily consistent provisioning of care to the orphans such as carrying, grooming, food sharing; Uehara and Nyundo, 1983; Goodall, 1986; Wroblewski, 2008; Boesch et al., 2010; Hobaiter et al., 2014; Samuni et al., 2019a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Uehara and Nyundo, 1983; Goodall, 1986; Wroblewski, 2008; Boesch et al., 2010; Hobaiter et al., 2014; Samuni et al., 2019a.

claim: The urine samples included in this study span over 19 years and were collected between 2000 and 2018.
source: The urine samples included in this study span over 19 years and were collected between 2000 and 2018 (see Table 1 for details about sample size).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and refers to data collection details.

claim: Recently orphaned individuals had a consistently steeper linear slope than non-orphans.
source: In the reduced model not comprising these two interaction terms, we found that recently orphaned individuals had a consistently steeper linear slope (estimate for the interaction between orphan status and the linear term for time of the day: –0.22, 95% CI: [–0.03: –0.48], P = 98.9%, Table 2, Figure 1, and Appendix 1—figure 1) than non-orphans.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the text and visualized in Figure 1.

claim: On average, recently orphaned individuals had a diurnal cortisol slope 58% steeper than non-orphans.
source: On average, recently orphaned individuals had a diurnal cortisol slope 58% steeper than non-orphans (average slope and [95% CI] for recently orphaned: –0.60 [-0.79: –0.41], and non-orphans: –0.38 [-0.53: –0.22]).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claim: Recently orphaned immatures had higher early morning cortisol levels as compared to non-orphan immatures.
source: A visual inspection of the model line prediction (Figure 1) indicates that this difference in slopes may stem from higher early morning cortisol levels in recently orphaned immatures as compared to non-orphan immatures (Figure 1 and Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: The claim is based on visual inspection of model predictions shown in Figure 1.

claim: There was no consistent difference between recently orphaned, not-recently orphaned, and non-orphans in their average cortisol levels at midday.
source: The 95% CI for the main effect of orphan status in the all immature model clearly overlapped 0, indicating that there was no consistent difference between recently orphaned, not-recently orphaned, and non-orphans in their average cortisol levels at midday.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claim: Recently orphaned individuals had higher cortisol levels in the morning and lower cortisol levels in the afternoon than non-orphans.
source: However, Figure 1 indicates that recently orphaned individuals had higher cortisol levels in the morning and lower cortisol levels in the afternoon than non-orphans.
evidence: The claim is based on visual inspection of Figure 1.

claim: Immature orphans whose mother had died several years before sampling had different diurnal cortisol slopes as compared to more recently orphaned immatures.
source: More specifically, and in line with the results of the all immature model, immature orphans whose mother had died several years before sampling had different diurnal cortisol slopes as compared to more recently orphaned immatures (estimate and [90% CI] for the interaction between years since maternal loss and the cubic term for time of day: –0.06 [-0.14: 0.00]).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claim: Immature orphans who lost their mother recently had higher cortisol levels throughout the day as compared to immature orphans who lost their mother several years ago.
source: A visual inspection of the data and the model prediction lines reveals that cortisol levels of immature orphans who recently lost their mother had higher cortisol levels throughout the day (orange squares in Figure 2) as compared to immature orphans who lost their mother several years ago (green triangles in Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is based on visual inspection of model predictions shown in Figure 2.

claim: The age at which immatures lost their mother consistently influenced their diurnal cortisol slopes and more specifically how it curved throughout the day.
source: In addition, in the immature orphan model, we found a consistent effect of the interaction between age when mother died and the quadratic term of time of day (estimate and [95% CI]: –0.12 [-0.23: –0.00], P- = 97.8%, Table 2), indicating that the age at which immatures lost their mother consistently influenced their diurnal cortisol slopes and more specifically how it curved throughout the day.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claim: Immature individuals who lost their mother before 5 years of age had a diurnal cortisol slope that curved upwards.
source: Immature individuals who lost their mother before 5 years of age (orange squares in Figure 3) had a diurnal cortisol slope that curved upwards.
evidence: The claim is based on visual inspection of model predictions shown in Figure 3.

claim: Immatures orphaned at a younger age presented higher early morning and late afternoon cortisol levels than individuals who lost their mother at an older age.
source: A visual inspection of the model prediction lines and the data points reveals that immatures orphaned at a younger age presented higher early morning and late afternoon cortisol levels than individuals who lost their mother at an older age.
evidence: The claim is based on visual inspection of model predictions shown in Figure 3.

claim: We did not detect a consistent effect of orphan status on mature males' diurnal cortisol profiles and cortisol levels.
source: In contrast to immature individuals, we did not detect a consistent effect of orphan status on mature males' diurnal cortisol profiles and cortisol levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claim: We did not detect a consistent effect of the age when mother died on orphan mature males' diurnal cortisol slopes and cortisol levels.
source: We also did not detect a consistent effect of the age when mother died on orphan mature males' diurnal cortisol slopes and cortisol levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claim: The effects of maternal loss on diurnal cortisol slopes in immature chimpanzees were neither present in individuals who lost their mothers more than 2 years earlier nor in mature male chimpanzees.
source: While we found an effect of maternal loss on diurnal cortisol slopes in immature chimpanzees whose mothers died recently (all immature and immature orphan models), these effects were neither present in individuals who lost their mothers more than 2 years earlier (all immature and immature orphan models) nor in mature male chimpanzees (adult male orphan model).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claim: The BEM may apply to long-lived wild mammals only following exposure to a combination of diverse sources of early-life adversity or to other sources of early-life adversity than maternal loss.
source: This suggests that the BEM (Power and Hertzman, 1997; Miller et al., 2011; Berens et al., 2017) may apply to long-lived wild mammals only following exposure to a combination of diverse sources of early-life adversity or to other sources of early-life adversity than maternal loss (see Rosenbaum et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study results and comparison with Rosenbaum et al., 2020.

claim: Amelioration in the social environment of immature chimpanzees, possibly in the form of buffering mechanisms ranging from minimal alloparental care to adoption, could modify the HPA axis activity of orphans throughout ontogeny and eventually ameliorate long-term effects of early-life adversity.
source: In the case of our study, amelioration in the social environment of immature chimpanzees, possibly in the form of buffering mechanisms ranging from minimal alloparental care to adoption (discussed below), could modify the HPA axis activity of orphans throughout ontogeny and eventually ameliorate long-term effects of early-life adversity.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about potential mechanisms.

claim: A survivorship bias may mean that chimpanzees with severely altered HPA axis activity following maternal loss did not survive to adulthood and thus were absent from our adult dataset.
source: Alternatively, in our study, a survivorship bias may mean that chimpanzees with severely altered HPA axis activity following maternal loss did not survive to adulthood and thus were absent from our adult dataset.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about potential bias in the data.

claim: Orphans experiencing maternal loss at younger ages had a diurnal cortisol slope differing from the immatures orphaned when older, particularly in the quadratic term for time of the day.
source: We also found that the age at maternal loss impacted the diurnal cortisol slopes of the orphans (immature orphan model). Orphans experiencing maternal loss at younger ages had a diurnal cortisol slope differing from the immatures orphaned when older, particularly in the quadratic term for time of the day (i.e., in how the slope curved).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claim: Orphans that lost their mother at younger ages had diurnal cortisol slopes that curved upwards towards the end of the day, whereas those that lost their mother later in ontogeny showed a more typical pattern observed in non-orphan immatures of more continual declines in their slopes.
source: Orphans that lost their mother at younger ages had diurnal cortisol slopes that curved upwards towards the end of the day, whereas those that lost their mother later in ontogeny showed a more typical pattern observed in non-orphan immatures of more continual declines in their slopes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the statistical analysis results.

claim: Orphans whom mother died early had higher early morning and late afternoon cortisol levels than those of immatures orphaned when older.
source: Visual inspection of the model lines and data points revealed that this difference in the slope led to higher early morning and late afternoon cortisol levels in orphan whom mother died early than in those of immatures orphaned when older.
evidence: The claim is based on visual inspection of model predictions.

claim: The diurnal cortisol slope of immature chimpanzees undergoes different levels of changes depending on the age at which they experience maternal loss, with more substantial deviations from mother-raised offspring pattern in immatures orphaned earlier in life.
source: In fact, diurnal cortisol slopes are indicative of the general functioning of the HPA axis (Karlamangla et al., 2019) and our results indicate that the diurnal cortisol slope of immature chimpanzees undergoes different levels of changes depending on the age at which they experience maternal loss, with more substantial deviations from mother-raised offspring pattern in immatures orphaned earlier in life.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study results and citation to Karlamangla et al., 2019.

claim: Recently orphaned immatures had a steeper rather than a flatter diurnal cortisol slopes compared to those of non-orphaned immatures.
source: However, this difference was only present for orphans who recently lost their mother, that is, within 2 years at the time of sampling. Furthermore, the direction of the effect was opposite to the prediction derived from the clinical human literature (Kaufman, 1991; Hart et al., 1996; Meinlschmidt and Heim, 2005; Dozier et al., 2006; Bernard et al., 2015; McLachlan et al., 2016) in that recently orphaned immatures had a steeper rather than a flatter diurnal cortisol slopes compared to those of non-orphaned immatures.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claim: The steeper slope in recently orphaned immatures is more likely to be driven by higher early morning cortisol levels rather than by lower late afternoon cortisol levels.
source: An inspection of the raw data (Figure 1 and Appendix 1—figure 1) reveals that this steeper slope is more likely to be driven by higher early morning cortisol levels rather than by lower late afternoon cortisol levels.
evidence: The claim is based on visual inspection of the data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Studies on humans and captive rats show that dietary restriction is associated with a rise in early morning cortisol levels.
source: Studies on humans and captive rats show that dietary restriction is associated with a rise in early morning cortisol levels (Goodwin et al., 1988; Garcia‐Belenguer et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Goodwin et al., 1988; Garcia‐Belenguer et al., 1993.

claim: Nutritional stress in orphan chimpanzees may result from the lack of access to food sources that were initially provided by the mother.
source: Nutritional stress in orphan chimpanzees may result from the lack of access to food sources that were initially provided by the mother (Pusey, 1983; Goldenberg and Wittemyer, 2017; Samuni et al., 2019a).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by citations to Pusey, 1983; Goldenberg and Wittemyer, 2017; Samuni et al., 2019a.

claim: Orphans may be constrained in acquiring the amount of food necessary to maintain a positive energy balance because orphans lack socially facilitated access to food sources previously provided by their mother and also miss out on maternal sharing of high nutrient food.
source: Although chimpanzees in our study were orphaned after weaning age (i.e., after 4 years of age, Samuni et al., 2020; Appendix 1—table 3), these orphans may nonetheless be constrained in acquiring the amount of food necessary to maintain a positive energy balance. This may be because orphans lack socially facilitated access to food sources previously provided by their mother and also miss out on maternal sharing of high nutrient food, such as meat, nuts, and honey, which occurs intermittently throughout ontogeny (Samuni et al., 2019a).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by citations to Samuni et al., 2020 and Samuni et al., 2019a.

claim: During the period directly following the loss of their mother, orphan chimpanzees might be exposed to acute stress, which modifies adaptively their HPA axis activity, allowing maintenance of homeostasis while developing and eventually survival until maturity, despite the potential lack of energy intake.
source: During the period directly following the loss of their mother, orphan chimpanzees might be exposed to acute stress, which modifies adaptively their HPA axis activity, allowing maintenance of homeostasis while developing and eventually survival until maturity, despite the potential lack of energy intake.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about adaptive mechanisms.

claim: In the same population, orphans lose out on growth compared to non-orphans.
source: For instance, in the same population, orphans lose out on growth compared to non-orphans (Samuni et al., 2020), which might result from reallocation of energy towards more vital functions (e.g., thermoregulation, muscle activity, general organismal functioning) than growth during energetically challenging periods.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Samuni et al., 2020.

claim: Play bouts involving orphan chimpanzees are shorter and more frequently escalate into aggression when compared to play bouts between non-orphans.
source: Play bouts involving orphan chimpanzees are shorter and more frequently escalate into aggression when compared to play bouts between non-orphans (Botero et al., 2013; Leeuwen et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Botero et al., 2013; Leeuwen et al., 2014.

claim: In chimpanzees and other primates aggression generally increases cortisol levels.
source: This could, in turn, lead to increased cortisol levels since in chimpanzees and other primates aggression generally increases cortisol levels (Girard-Buttoz et al., 2009; Emery Thompson et al., 2010; Wittig et al., 2015; but see Preis et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Girard-Buttoz et al., 2009; Emery Thompson et al., 2010; Wittig et al., 2015; but see Preis et al., 2019.

claim: Mothers are the main social partners of immature chimpanzees.
source: Mothers are the main social partners of immature chimpanzees Reddy and Sandel, 2020; therefore, orphan chimpanzees lack access to a key source of social buffering from environmental stressors (Young et al., 2014; Wittig et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Reddy and Sandel, 2020.

claim: Orphan chimpanzees lack access to a key source of social buffering from environmental stressors.
source: Mothers are the main social partners of immature chimpanzees Reddy and Sandel, 2020; therefore, orphan chimpanzees lack access to a key source of social buffering from environmental stressors (Young et al., 2014; Wittig et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the fact that mothers are main social partners and citations to Young et al., 2014; Wittig et al., 2016.

claim: The effects of maternal loss on chimpanzees' physiology do not persist into adulthood.
source: As in humans, maternal loss impacts the physiology of immature chimpanzees. However, the effects of maternal loss on chimpanzees' physiology differ strongly from that of humans, in that they do not persist into adulthood.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claim: Immatures that were orphaned for more than 2 years had cortisol excretion profiles that were not consistently different from the profiles of non-orphans.
source: More strikingly, immatures that were orphaned for more than 2 years had cortisol excretion profiles that were not consistently different from the profiles of non-orphans.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claim: The re-establishment of a normal functioning of the HPA axis in mature male chimpanzees but also in immatures orphaned for more than 2 years may reflect a form of recovery in those individuals.

claim: The lack of apparent long-term effects of maternal loss on immature chimpanzee physiology could be indicative of ameliorations in the environment of these orphans in the years following maternal loss, possibly in terms of improved access to social support and food.

claim: Adoption is a relatively common phenomenon in chimpanzees.
source: In chimpanzees, adoption is a relatively common phenomenon (Uehara and Nyundo, 1983; Goodall, 1986; Wroblewski, 2008; Boesch et al., 2010; Hobaiter et al., 2014; Samuni et al., 2019a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Uehara and Nyundo, 1983; Goodall, 1986; Wroblewski, 2008; Boesch et al., 2010; Hobaiter et al., 2014; Samuni et al., 2019a.

claim: Adopters typically provide surrogate care for the orphan in the form of grooming, limited provisioning through food sharing, agonistic support, nest sharing, and even carrying.
source: Adopters typically provide surrogate care for the orphan in the form of grooming, limited provisioning through food sharing, agonistic support, nest sharing, and even carrying (Samuni et al., 2019a).

claim: Long-term alteration of the HPA axis functioning related to early-life adversity is explained, at least partly, by epigenetic mechanisms and in particular by a hyper-methylation of DNA in regions coding for the glucocorticoid receptors (GRs) in the brain.
source: Long-term alteration of the HPA axis functioning related to early-life adversity is explained, at least partly, by epigenetic mechanisms (Weaver et al., 2004) and in particular by a hyper-methylation of DNA in regions coding for the glucocorticoid receptors (GRs) in the brain (Liu et al., 1997; Weaver et al., 2007, reviewed in Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Weaver et al., 2004; Liu et al., 1997; Weaver et al., 2007, reviewed in Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: In rodents tested in laboratory conditions, alterations of the GR in the brain take place early in life; a lower density of GR reduces the effectiveness of the glucocorticoid-negative feedback loop and ultimately results in prolonged elevated cortisol levels.
source: In rodents tested in laboratory conditions, these alterations of the GR in the brain take place early in life; a lower density of GR reduces the effectiveness of the glucocorticoid-negative feedback loop and ultimately results in prolonged elevated cortisol levels (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: Modifications of the HPA axis activation may have some fitness consequences in wild mammalian populations.
source: Even though modifications of the HPA axis activation may have some fitness consequences in wild mammalian populations (Campos et al., 2021), this mechanism is unlikely to explain the lower reproductive fitness and survival observed in adult male orphan chimpanzees (Nakamura et al., 2014; Crockford et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Campos et al., 2021.

claim: This mechanism is unlikely to explain the lower reproductive fitness and survival observed in adult male orphan chimpanzees.

evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study results and citations to Nakamura et al., 2014; Crockford et al., 2020.

source: In fact, in our study male orphans who reach adulthood do not present cortisol excretion profiles that differ from those of non-orphans.

claim: The modification in the HPA axis activity during the two first years following maternal loss found in our study might mediate fitness-related costs such as slowed growth rather than directly resulting in negative fitness outcomes.
source: While modifications of HPA axis activity are unlikely to directly impact chimpanzee fitness in adult individuals, the modification in the HPA axis activity during the two first years following maternal loss found in our study might mediate fitness-related costs such as slowed growth (Samuni et al., 2020) rather than directly resulting in negative fitness outcomes.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by a citation to Samuni et al., 2020.
